Café membership revamp brief

A café product brief with six numbered decisions, a customer journey, a before-and-after impact table, and the risks, acceptance criteria, and scope on one warm-toned page.

Read the source prompt
Create a warm narrative product brief. Preserve the following headings and exact copy. Eyebrow: “Product brief · café”. Title: “Café membership revamp”. Subtitle: “A brief for the café membership app: decisions first, then flow and impact.” ☕ Decision-first / The revamp in six decisions: 01 · R1 Stars, not points: Every yuan spent earns one star; no thresholds, no expiry. 02 · R2 Three tiers: Your rolling 90-day total sets silver, gold, or black-gold tiers. 03 · R3 One-scan checkout: A single scan earns stars and redeems rewards; it works offline. 04 · R4 Store value gifts: Load 200, get 20. Refundable, with the rules on the home page. 05 · R5 Birthday doubles: All purchases in the birthday week earn twice the stars. 06 · R6 Trends, not profiles: The store dashboard shows trends only, not per-customer profiles. ⭐️ Customer flow / One order, four steps: ☕️ Order: In person at the counter, or in the app. → ⭐️ Earn: Stars are credited after one scan. → 📈 Level up: 90 days sets your tier. → 🎁 Redeem: Stars trade for treats. 🧾 Impact / What changes for whom: Audience | Today | After the revamp; Regulars | Paper stamp cards, lost means gone | Stars live in the app, visible forever; Baristas | Stamp by hand, reconcile monthly | One scan covers earning and redemption; Managers | Manual membership counts at month end | Live sales trends in the dashboard; Bookkeeping | Stored value on notebook ledgers | Balances and gifts post automatically. ⚠️ Dependency / Risks and dependencies: Paper stamp cards convert into the app by the end of October, running in parallel for two weeks. If conversion slips, the new rules start a week later; store events are unchanged. ✅ Acceptance / Definition of done: ✓ A regular earns and redeems stars in a single scan; ✓ Tier changes on the 90-day total apply automatically; ✓ Baristas record offline; uploads resume on reconnect; ✓ Stored value refunds to the original payment method; 🚫 Boundary / Non-goals for this revamp: × Delivery and takeout; × Social feeds and comments; × Cross-store shared points; × Ad slots and co-branding; Footer label: “Decision owners”. Footer: “R1–R3 product, R4–R5 store ops, R6 data. Payment compliance sign-off is required before R4 ships. All names and figures are synthetic sample data.” Export PNG, standalone HTML, and the complete Diagram JSON.

Architectureeditorial

From agent input to local rendering

The agent handles source text under its own privacy settings; Diagram JSON is rendered into local files.

Read the source prompt
Create an editorial layered architecture overview explaining text2html2png. A prompt and source facts enter the chosen agent, which may use a remote service under its own privacy settings. The agent selects a chart and style, preserves the supplied facts, and writes Diagram JSON. The local Node.js runtime generates and validates self-contained HTML, and local Chrome audits the layout. HTML is the default output; PNG is exported only on explicit request. The renderer has no telemetry and blocks browser network requests by default. Clearly distinguish agent processing from local rendering; do not claim the whole conversation stays on the machine.

Architectureclean

Order Events: Requests, Ownership, and Delivery

A synthetic technical case with synchronous requests, asynchronous event routes, explicit database ownership, and delivery boundaries. Arrows indicate layers, not individual dependencies.

Read the source prompt
Create a clean architecture grouping diagram for this synthetic order-system case, and also export PNG. This is an illustrative design, not a real customer system or a benchmark. Use three layers: entry points, services, and resources. The storefront synchronously calls the order service to create an order. The payment platform synchronously calls the payment callback service with a callback ID. The order service alone reads and writes its own PostgreSQL database: it commits an order and its outbox record together, then its publisher sends OrderCreated to the event queue. It also consumes PaymentConfirmed from that queue, updating payment status and recording the consumed event ID in one transaction. The callback service alone reads and writes a separate PostgreSQL database: it commits the callback ID and its outbox record together, acknowledges after commit, and its publisher sends PaymentConfirmed to the same queue. The inventory consumer receives OrderCreated and alone reads and writes a third PostgreSQL database, committing the reservation and consumed event ID together. Queue delivery is at least once: OrderCreated goes only to the inventory consumer; PaymentConfirmed goes only to the order service. Failed publishing is retried from each service's outbox. Callback IDs deduplicate callbacks; consumed event IDs deduplicate consumption. Mark all three databases and their exclusive owners, keep synchronous and asynchronous relationships explicit, and retain these delivery boundaries. Layer arrows indicate grouping only, not node-to-node wiring or a serial call chain. Do not add a gateway, cloud vendor, throughput, latency, or an exactly-once guarantee.

Comparisonclean

Choosing a plan

Three plan tiers aligned row by row on one shared set of criteria, with no invented winner.

Read the source prompt
Make a clean comparison of three plans — Community, Team, Studio — on the same criteria: seats included, active projects, storage, support response, monthly price, annual price. Community: 3 seats, 5 projects, 2 GB, community forum only, $0; describe it as self-hosted, for solo work and evaluation. Team: 25 seats, 50 projects, 100 GB, 1 business day, $18 per seat monthly, $180 per seat annually; describe it as shared projects for a small group. Studio: unlimited seats and projects, 1 TB, 4 hours, $49 per seat monthly, $490 per seat annually; describe it as for larger groups that need a response time. Annual billing charges ten months per seat. Close with a short "how to read it" note: seats and projects are hard caps, support response is the target time to a first reply during business hours and Community has no target, and the ten-month rule is why $18 becomes $180 and $49 becomes $490. Title it "Choosing a plan" and do not declare a winner.

Make your first diagram

1. Install the skill

Run this in your terminal. Use Node.js 22.12+ and an installed Chrome-family browser. The agent installs the local runtime dependencies when needed.

npx skills add GODVvVZzz/text2html2png -g -y

2. Send a prompt to your agent

Copy a prompt from an example above, replace the description with your own, and send it to Codex, Claude Code, or another compatible agent.

HTML is the default deliverable. The copied prompt explicitly asks for PNG too. Keep the JSON to revise the content and render again.

Try the renderer locally

Edit Diagram JSON, preview, and export in your browser. This local playground does not convert free-form text; your agent handles that step.

git clone https://github.com/GODVvVZzz/text2html2png.git
cd text2html2png/skills/text2html2png
npm start

What keeps the result useful

Keep the supplied facts

The skill instructs the agent to preserve facts and relationships, and omit unsupported metrics. Review the meaning against your source before sharing.

Check the actual layout

The browser audit checks clipping, overlap, contrast, and short Chinese labels. PNG export runs the audit before capturing the image.

Keep your source

HTML, PNG, and versioned Diagram JSON are files you can keep. Rendering runs locally; your agent’s handling of input depends on its service.

Architecture examples show layers; node descriptions state the specific dependencies. Use a graph editor for arbitrary node-to-node connections. Use a plotting library for scientific charts.
